At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 423.5 was anchored closely to recent trading levels, assuming no major overnight developments and typical mean-reverting intraday behavior. For the one-week estimate of 426, I incorporated a slight positive bias reflecting the general long-run upward drift in equity markets, while still keeping the estimate close to current levels given the short window. The one-month estimate of 432 extended that same drift assumption further, implying roughly a 2% gain consistent with historical average monthly returns for broad equity indices or similar instruments, while remaining conservative enough not to overstate directional conviction.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, historical daily volatility in the underlying asset — typically in the range of 1–2% for an instrument priced around 420 — justified a relatively tight band of roughly plus or minus 15 points. Over one week, I scaled that volatility by the square root of time, producing a wider band of about plus or minus 30 points. By one month, the interval expanded to roughly plus or minus 60 points, reflecting not just scaled volatility but also the increased likelihood of regime-changing events accumulating over a longer period. Implied volatility conditions, liquidity dynamics, and the asset's recent realized volatility all factored into calibrating these widths.

Several risks could push outcomes outside these intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharper-than-expected jobs report, a surprise in inflation readings, or escalating geopolitical tensions — could produce a sharp selloff exceeding the lower bounds. A sudden shift in central bank communication, particularly from the Federal Reserve, could reprice risk assets quickly and meaningfully. On the upside, stronger-than-expected earnings, a dovish policy pivot, or a resolution of ongoing geopolitical uncertainty could drive prices well above the upper bounds of my intervals, particularly at the one-month horizon where the compounding of positive catalysts has more room to operate.

It is also worth noting that tail risks are by nature asymmetric and hard to quantify precisely. Black swan events — whether financial contagion, a sudden credit event, or unexpected geopolitical escalation — could produce moves of 10% or more in a short period, which would fall entirely outside even my widest stated interval.
